source.title: Unsupervised Elicitation of Language Models
source.authors: Jia-Xin Wen; Zachary Ankner; Arushi Somani; P. Hase; Samuel Marks; Jacob Goldman-Wetzler; Linda Petrini; Henry Sleight; Collin Burns; He He; Shi Feng; Ethan Perez; Jan Leike

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses weak-to-strong generalization, but its method uses labels generated through internal coherence maximization rather than labels from a weaker supervisor. Its results therefore do not test the stated weak-to-strong claim or its listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper says unsupervised elicitation can be viewed as a special case of weak-to-strong generalization, but also distinguishes its approach as ignoring weak supervision. The adjacent ICM results below use model-generated labels, not a weaker model as supervisor; they do not measure PGR. Other reported ICM results are not included as claim-version tests.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces ICM, which fine-tunes a pretrained model on labels it generates itself, with no external or weaker-model supervision. It cites weak-to-strong generalization only as related framing, calling ICM a special case that ignores weak supervision. Its baselines are golden labels, crowdsourced human labels, and labels distilled from GPT-4o, a stronger model. None is a weaker-model supervisor, and no PGR or weak-supervisor-versus-student comparison is reported. The human-label results (e.g., gender prediction, human accuracy 60%) concern human supervision of a strong model. They are not reported as student-versus-supervisor gaps, and no version names human supervisors.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that ICM matches golden-label training and beats crowdsourced human labels on several tasks. It fails on non-salient concepts such as the sun-poem task. An ICM-trained reward model used to RL-train a Claude 4 Sonnet assistant matches a human-supervised counterpart on average: better on chat and safety, worse on math and code. They frame unsupervised elicitation as a special case of weak-to-strong generalization that ignores weak supervision altogether.
record.recipe_differences: ICM searches for labels using mutual predictability and logical consistency rather than training a strong model on labels supplied by a weaker supervisor; it does not measure PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that ICM performance varies with model capability, task, and data size; it also reports task-dependent effects of removing logical consistency. These are ICM results, not weak-to-strong PGR results.

fits_no_version.finding: ICM self-generated labels match golden-label fine-tuning on GSM8K-verification and TruthfulQA and exceed crowdsourced human labels on Alpaca and gender prediction (Table 3, Figs 3 and 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised elicitation (internal coherence maximization) can match golden supervision on tasks salient to the pretrained model.

record.problems: The reported adjacent results concern ICM, not weak-supervisor fine-tuning or PGR. The paper notes that ICM cannot elicit concepts that are not salient to the pretrained model; some results are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Other ICM experiments, including figures on scaling, initialization, logical-consistency ablations, and reward-model evaluation, were left out because they do not test the weak-to-strong claim or a listed version.

untested.parts: Strong student trained on a weaker model's labels versus that supervisor; PGR.
Training changes that raise PGR over naive fine-tuning on weak labels.
PGR dependence on supervisor and student size, task, or representations.
Exploitation of a weak supervisor, PGR under distribution shift, shared errors.
Theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: No weaker-model supervisor appears anywhere in the study. The GPT-4o distillation baseline uses a stronger, post-trained model. Human-label baselines involve human supervision, which the versions do not name, and no PGR is computed. The reader's T6/discusses classification is kept.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a strong student trained on a weaker model's labels beats that supervisor; PGR.
Whether training changes improve PGR over naive fine-tuning on weak-supervisor labels.
PGR variation by weak-supervisor and student size, task, or representations.
The specified weak-to-strong failure modes, including distribution shift and shared errors.
Theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.
Weak-to-strong generalization outside language, including vision.
